name: Ser Aldric Vane
appearance: Beautiful in a severe way. Of the two boys who once held other men's horses together he is the one with the better seat and the better manners, and at Harrow Ford he sat his horse at Darrow's left hand, close enough to touch, with his eyes on the far bank; told he looked like a man at his own wedding, he didn't smile. He spends few words. The ones he gave Darrow at the ford were a warning: ride wide, then wider, and whatever came next went unsaid when the chaplain's bell began.
last_seen_doing: Bent low over his horse's neck on the west bank of the Wend, the horse already turned and already climbing out, as Darrow went under midriver; by Darrow's count, one heartbeat early.
now: Offstage since Harrow Ford, where Darrow last saw him on the west bank as the river closed over him. Seven weeks after the Binding, with six grey cloaks and a censer on the Holloway, Darrow believes that the hand that wrote his name first on their list was that of the man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys; the page has only Wren's silence and her look to say who was first.
story_so_far: He and Darrow were squires together, holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel with their palms on the same warming stone. At Harrow Ford he had the Second Lance, held in reserve by the writ from command, and sat at Darrow's left hand on the west bank watching the far shore, telling him to ride wide, and then wider, with some other word left unsaid in his open mouth when the chaplain's bell cut him off. When the Grace went out of the Ninth midriver and Darrow went under, the last thing Darrow saw through the spray was Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned, already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck; when the red-handed woman turned his head back to the water, the Second sat its horses in perfect order, untouched, watching. Seven weeks later, with grey cloaks on the Holloway and a list of the Faithless, Darrow thought of a man in a warm room in Calden writing a name, and heard again: Ride wide today.

known_facts.fact: He has the Second Lance, which the writ from command held in reserve while the Sixth and the Ninth were sent to clear the ford, and he sat his horse at Darrow's left hand, close enough to touch, on the west bank of Harrow Ford.

He and Darrow rode knee to knee from the time they were squires holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel, kneeling shoulder to shoulder with their palms on the Oathstone while it warmed under their hands.
Darrow still remembers his face when the Grace went into him the first time: like a man hearing music he had only ever been told about.
By Darrow's account he has the better seat, the better manners and the better luck with the kind of women whose fathers mattered.

Before the crossing he watched the far bank without smiling and told Darrow to ride wide, then wider; his mouth was open on some other word when the chaplain's bell began down the line, and he shut it and looked away.

As Darrow went under, he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank already turned and already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck, one heartbeat early by Darrow's count; when the red-handed woman turned Darrow's head to the river, the Second Lance sat its horses on the west bank in perfect order, untouched, watching.

On the night Maelis offered Darrow the two ways off the mountain, he thought of the field-stone warming under his palm and of Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned, before he asked whether he could kneel after.

With Darrow's name first on the list the Confessors read out at the inn in Coldmere, Darrow believes it was written in a warm room in Calden by a man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys, and hears again the words "Ride wide today."
